speakeroldname: Mr. Simon de Jong (Regina East) moved:
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INCOME TAX PROVISION OF FUNDING FOR PEACE
speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation whereby the income tax form would provide a specific section enabling taxpayes, who so indicate, to have that percentage of total annual federal expenditures dedicated to national defence transferred to a peace tax trust which would provide funding for peace and disarmament research and education.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today on a timely issue of concern to us all, the survival of the human species. We live in a world where the two major powers have built up an arsenal of nuclear, chemical and biological destruction. In terms of the nuclear dimension alone, each superpower has the capacity to kill every man, woman and child 14 times over. It is totally unthinkable to even contemplate a global nuclear war. The lucky ones will be those who are killed immediately in such a confrontation.
Recently we have heard about the effects of a nuclear winter. Noteworthy scientists from both superpowers have predicted that a nuclear war would set off a nuclear winter that would destroy our weather patterns totally and make it impossible to grow crops and feed the remaining population. Nuclear war would destroy totally the social and physical connections within our country. Communication, electricity and gas lines would be totally disrupted along with our social network of hospitals and policing.
Of course, there are the long-term effects of nuclear war, including genetic mutations. In our age of increased nuclear testing above ground we saw dramatic increases in leukemia throughout the world.
There are generals from both major powers who suggest that a nuclear war is plausible and that a limited nuclear war can be won. Such a suggestion is unthinkable.
Let me quote from Lord Mountbatten who was actively involved in the two great wars as a commander. He stated on May 11, 1979:
As a military man who has given half a century of active service I say in all sincerity that the nuclear arms race has no military purpose. Wars cannot be fought with nuclear weapons. Their existence only adds to our perils because of the illusions which they have generated.
There are powerful voices around the world who still give credence of the old Roman precept-if you desire peace, prepare for war. This is absolute nuclear nonsense and I repeat-it is a disastrous misconception to believe that by increasing the total uncertainty one increases one's own certainty.
Despite the warnings of people like Lord Mountbatten, the arms race continues unabated. What makes rational human beings become involved in an arms race from which no one can emerge a winner? Surely it must be a sense of paranoia that

March 10, 1986
Income Tax
exists both in the United States and the Soviet Union. In many ways, this paranoia is understandable.
Let us put ourselves in the position of the Soviet Union which has historically been surrounded by opposing forces. The Soviet Union is totally surrounded with nuclear warheads, missiles and submarines and is a country that lost many of its citizens in the last war. From that perspective, the origin of its paranoia is quite understandable.
When we put ourselves in the position of the United States, as most of us in the western world do, we certainly have a basis for fearing the might of the Soviet Union. We have seen how the Soviets have expanded their borders into Afghanistan, Poland and Czechoslovakia. While the origin of our paranoia may be understandable, we have reached the point where the paranoia of one nation feeds on the paranoia of the other, like two images reflecting in a mirror. The Soviets become paranoid as they seee Cruise missiles and stronger weapons being situated around their borders. Therefore, they take what they consider to be protective steps, through increased defences, which is perceived by the western world as an offensive build-up. Therefore, we increase our defence expenditures which leads to increased Soviet defence expenditures, and the spiral continues.
Surely we have reached the point today when the very survival of the human race stands at the brink, when enough armaments have been built up on both sides that a mistake, a misconception or a mad act can offset a chain of events that will totally destroy the human race as we know it.
Therefore, as parliamentarians, wherever we may live, there is no greater issue than the survival of our human race.
Let me introduce another dimension into this debate. It is the economic dimension. Conservative estimates indicate that the total cost of the arms race is close to three-quarters of a trillion dollars. It is not possible to remove a trillion dollars from the economy of the world without everyone paying for it.
We pay for it in terms of higher interest rates. For example, the American deficit is almost a trillion dollars, largely due to the arms race. It is so great that total U.S. savings hardly meet the interest on that deficit. Therefore, the United States must maintain a strong American dollar in order to attract capital from other parts of the world and service their debt. In order for Canada to keep some of that capital we must also raise our interest rates.
Interest rates are normally 2 per cent to 3 per cent above the inflation rate. Therefore, with inflation currently at 4 per cent, interest rates should be approximately 7 per cent. At 7 per cent, a lot of farms will be able to survive along with a lot of small businesses. A lot of people will be able to afford to buy a new car or a new home. All this economic activity could occur if it were not for the high interest rates. [DOT]
I maintain that every Canadian on a day-to-day basis pays
for the arms race through higher interest rates, unemployment
and farm bankruptcies. We cannot take a $1 trillion dollars
out of the world economy without the result of lower standards of living for all people throughout the world, Canadians, Americans, Russians and Europeans. It is a reduction of $1 trillion to all of our standards of living. That is the price we pay for this madness which any reasonable person must admit does not work. If these weapons are ever actually used it will mean our mutual destruction. What my motion is asking today is that those conscientious objectors, any Canadian who feels that our participation in this madness is not a very fruitful exercise, those people who feel, because if their religious beliefs and moral principles, that their tax dollars should not help to contribute to this dance of death, be allowed to have their money put in a peace trust.
The history of conscientious objectors is an honourable one stretching through the history of the human race. There are groups of people who believe that participating in wars and in the arms race is not the solution to the problems which create war. Some of us might disagree with that, but no reasonable person can object to allowing those members of our society to object in a conscientious way to the machinery of killing. It would enrich our civilization and make us as a more civilized society if we allowed those men and women, because of their consciences, to object to participating in this madness. I am asking for this for those enlightened Canadians who believe that more can be obtained to satisfy the security needs of Canada if we spend more money on peace research and find out how we can resolve the human conflicts which create war. Such things as checking up on compliance, what is the proper technology for that? It needs money, research, investment to develop educational programs so that people can stop thinking in terms of the "good guy-bad guy" scenario but will think, rather, in terms of co-operating. Those are the models which are needed if we are going to resolve the conflicts which create this potential for war.
There is a tremendous need for peace research. The only way we can save our civilization and our way of life is through peace. Yet that hardly receives any funding at all. I believe it is close to $300,000 per year. Of course, our military budget is much closer to $9 billion per year. As a country, we spend over $9 billion doing things which I would tend to think most Members of Parliament in their heart of hearts really believe is a futile effort. There is no defence in a nuclear age, only madness. But we continue to pour over $9 billion into this make-believe.
But there is an area in which we can have some effect, an area which can really help to preserve and save our way of life, that is, peace research, to which we now only give a token amount. I am asking for the support of my colleagues. I ask them to look favourably upon my motion and to pass it.
The Conscious Canada organization is not unique. There are some 17 countries with similar organizations. In fact, they have achieved some success in various jurisdictions. In Italy, some 17 taxpayers who had been charged with not paying their taxes because of conscientious objections, have been found by the Italian courts to be not quilty. Under the Italian Constitution, they are guaranteed the right of conscience. In the United
March 10, 1986

Kingdom, Some 20,000 individuals, including 60 Members of Parliament, have a signed a document urging the Government to change its legislation to allow the people to not pay that proportion of their taxes which would go to military spending, and instead have it redirected to peace research. In the United States, the peace tax fund Bill is supported by 42 Members of Congress and four Senators. So the story goes through some 17 countries where there are organized groups of individuals who are attempting to redirect their tax money towards peace research.
1 urge the Government to play a leadership role and Canada can play this very vital role. But here we stand between the two superpowers, the Soviet Union and the United States. Our very survival is dependent upon peace. It is dependent on the hope that those powers do not use their weapons of destruction, because if they do, it will happen over our heads. It is in our immediate national interest to maintain peace so, therefore, it must be in our national interest to do everything possible to work towards peace and disarmament, to make certain that those two superpowers remain at peace with each other.
I ask my hon. colleagues to support me in my motion so that Canada can take its rightful place and play its rightful role as a peacemaker in this world and to do that not only in our national interests but in the interests of the whole human race.
Humanity cries for a country and a group of people to rise up and take that leadership role. I urge my colleagues to dare to be different. I urge them to state that the king is wearing no clothes, that the arms race is a make-believe world filled with tremendous fear and danger. 1 challenge my colleagues to stand up and dare to be different in this world and to help preserve the human race.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Landry (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INCOME TAX PROVISION OF FUNDING FOR PEACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is further to the proposal of the Hon. Member for Regina Est (Mr. de Jong) for allocating income tax revenues to funding for peace and disarmament research and education. The Hon. Member is no doubt aware that according to one of the fundamental principles of our society, Canadians elect Members to speak on their behalf when decisions are made on matters such as the allocation of financial resources that are supposed to benefit all members of our society. In its present form, the Income Tax Act contains no provision that allows taxpayers to determine areas to which their taxes are to be allocated.
Any change in the allocation of personal income tax revenues, such as the proposal contains, requires an amendment to the Income Tax Act by an Act of Parliament.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is responsible both for proposing and amending tax legislation and will deal with the tax questions raised by this motion.
In any case, today, Canadians can actually obtain tax deductions by making donations to non-profit Canadian peace
Income Tax
organizations appearing in directories such as "A Directory of Canadian Peace Organizations with International Concerns", published by the Mennonite Central Committee.
The Government believes that defence and peace activities are not mutually exclusive, and that an amendment to the Income tax Act is unnecessary, since Government expenditures can be balanced so as to safeguard the security of Canada and the Alliance, while at the same time taking advantage of every reasonable opportunity to advance the cause of arms control and disarmament and of world peace and security.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may explain how Canada is now advancing the cause of peace and security without having to de-allocate tax revenues earmarked for defence in order to subsidize organizations for peace research and education.
For 35 years, our security policy has been based on three complementary principles: Deterrence, within the context of the collective security provisions of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the North American Air Defense Command; seeking fair and genuine agreements on arms control; and finally, a commitment to peaceful resolution of disputes, including participation in collective efforts to deal with the underlying social, economic and political causes of international tension.
Canada recognizes the need for collective action to discourage acts of aggression against North America and Europe. It endorses and financially supports NATO's defence efforts, particularly those policies under which the Alliance must have as few as possible of the weapons required for effective deterrence, while at the same time seeking to establish a dialogue and reach fair, balanced and verifiable arms control agreements. In that respect, stability and security for all are the objectives.
We belong to an Alliance whose deterrence strategy rests on both conventional and nuclear forces. Deterrence must guarantee enough stability to enable us to negotiate international agreements on arms control. Each member of the Alliance must share the burden of collective defence while benefiting from its protection. Our direct contribution to deterrence and defence is to provide efficient conventional forces. Rather than a question of ethics, it is a matter of knowing how we can best contribute to our own security, taking our limited resources into account.
The Government has clearly indicated its intention of honouring its commitments to our allies in terms of contributing to the stability of East-West relations with respect to security, and this stability flows from a credible and effective deterrence position. We have decided to provide a defence budget which is big enough to guarantee the effectiveness of our contribution and reduce the vulnerability of our troops in the field. In short, Mr. Speaker, an effective defence paves the way to peace.

March 10, 1986
Income Tax
It must be said however that defence funds are used to finance various nonmilitary measures which directly benefit all Canadians and contribute to restoring peace. This brings to mind the planning activities of Emergency Canada. As to our armed forces, they perform a great many nonmilitary roles such as the evacuation of critically flood-striken communities, search and rescue operations, fishing patrols, air transport of supplies and medical assistance to countries hit by natural disasters like earthquakes, as well as many other emergency services.
As a sovereign nation, Canada must dedicate part of its resources to develop and maintain its defence capability. At the same time, it is second to none among nations for its efforts in promoting disarmament and arms control, as well as international peace and security.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal now with the six Canadian goals in arms control and disarmament, as spelled out on October 31 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) before the Consultative Group on Disarmament and Arms Control Affairs, and more recently by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) in his speech before the House on January 23. They are: First, negotiated radical reductions in nuclear forces and the enhancement of strategic stability. Second, maintenance and strengthening of the nuclear non proliferation regime. Third, negotiation of global chemical weapons ban. Fourth, support for a comprehensive test ban treaty. Fifth, prevention of an arms race in outer space. Sixth, the building of confidence sufficient to facilitate the reduction of military forces in Europe and elsewhere.
Concerning the first objective, the Canadian Government welcomes the progress made in the bilateral negotiations held in Geneva between the United States and the Soviet Union. We fully support the goals agreed upon and deem as encouraging the detailed proposals made last fall by both parties. These proposals have certain points in common, Mr. Speaker, but like all Canadians, we fervently hope that negotiations will bring about fair and verifiable reductions of nuclear weapons.
In his statement of January 23, the Secretary of State for External Affairs welcomed with satisfaction the latest proposal of Secretary General Gorbatchev, who reaffirmed the commitment of the Soviet Union to nuclear disarmament. While this new proposal is silent on certain issues, such as the SS-20 missiles now deployed in Asia, it does provide some encouragement.
The second objective mentioned by the Secretary of State is the maintenance and consolidation of the non-proliferation regime. Last year, Canada took part in the Third Nuclear Weapons Non-proliferation Treaty Review Conference, which was a great success for all the countries. Indeed, the countries present at the Conference reaffirmed by consensus the viability of the Non-proliferation Treaty as an essential tool in maintaining world security. The success of this review process shows that multilateral diplomacy can have results when all
the parties involved decide to cooperate instead of confronting each other. Canada confirms this success since two major objectives have been reached, namely the maintenance of the NPT as the main foundation of the non-proliferation regime and confirmation of the objective and provisions of the NPT.
The complete ban of chemical weapons is our third objective. We believe that this can be achieved at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva. To support the ongoing negotiations, Canada has shared the knowledge it acquired following investigation of the use of chemical weapons and presented last year to the Secretary General of the United Nations a manual on how to carry out this type of investigation.
The fourth item on which Canada is working is the bringing about of a total ban on testing. Support for such a ban is a basic goal of Canada's foreign policy. However, it is our belief that the question of inspection is the major obstacle to be overcome. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has announced in September, 1985, at the meeting of the United Nations' General Assembly, that Canada would update its analytical capacity in the area of seismic research. To that end, we intend to enhance our major facilities in Yellowknife in order to be in a position to better discriminate between low-amplitude earthquakes from disturbances caused by underground nuclear testing.
In addition to that, Canada took part with 26 other countries in the international exchange of seismological data. That technical experiment has been a major step on the road towards the verifiability of a total ban of tests.
The fifth goal, that is the prevention of the arms race in outer space, is now on the agenda of bilateral talks in Geneva. In the multilateral context, Canada took the lead at the 1985 session of the Disarmament Conference held in Geneva by circulating a discussion paper on the International Law Aspects of Outer Space, thereby contributing to the substance of the discussion.
As a final goal, this Government feels it is critical to develop the measures of confidence required to bring about a reduction of armed forces in Europe and elsewhere. Confidence is fostered by political actions conducive to increased East-West co-operation, and strengthening the dialogue is one of Canada's major goals.
Peacekeeping is another key component of the efforts to establish international peace and security. One of the goals of Canada's foreign policy has always been to help strengthen the powers of the United Nations Organization, especially its capacity to control conflicts and act as mediator. This goal, which has been part of our general aim to work for peace and security, remains a valid one. In fact, it is in our own interests to stop regional conflicts before they can escalate and jeopardize our security or vital interests. Our military role in international peacekeeping operations helps prevent hostilities from
March 10, 1986

spreading or breaking out, so that the underlying political problems can be dealt with through negotiations and the threat of direct involvement by the super powers kept to a minimum. Elowever, Canada has never considered peacekeeping as a goal unto itself. Peacekeeping is aimed not only at preventing conflicts but also at creating a climate conducive to seeking solutions to the underlying problems. That is why Canada has always held the view that there should be considerable emphasis on the link between peacekeeping and the efforts deployed by all parties concerned to achieve peace.
Since 1947, Canada has participated in 15 UN peacekeeping operations. Outside the UN context, we have taken part in three similar missions, namely, the control commissions of 1954 and 1973 in Indochina and the international observers group in Nigeria. These initiatives were mostly financed from the Defence budget. During the past financial year, the Government of Canada has contributed over $41 million towards military salaries paid by the United Nations. These operations reflect the profound commitment and continuing contribution of generations of Canadians and successive governments to the peace objective.
Mr. Speaker, through various UN agencies, the Government has made a continuing contribution towards maintaining peace in all the countries of this world.
Not long ago, the Government demonstrated its commitment to peacekeeping. On April 11 last year, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that Canada agreed in principle to take part in the multinational force and observers group based in the Sinai peninsula. The departments concerned are now considering how Canada can best contribute to the operations of the force, to replace the Australian helicopter unit of 100 men which is due to be withdrawn in April 1986.
Mr. Speaker, 1 would now like to consider the means available to the Government to give direct support to organizations involved in peace research and education, and thus provide an argument against setting up the peace tax trust proposed by the Hon. Member for Regina-Est (Mr. de Jong).
During the current fiscal year, over $700,000 from the External Affairs Canada's Disarmament Fund will be made available to groups and individuals from all parts of Canada. Since its creation in 1980-81, the Fund has made it possible for over 149 groups, organizations and individuals to support and encourage the debate, research and supply of information on all issues related to disarmament and arms control.
The Department of External Affairs subsidizes also other research and public information activities in this area. The Verification Section of the Arms Control and Disarmament Division is responsible for the analysis of the verification process and developing techniques and approaches for verifi-cating the enforcement of current and future arms control and disarmament agreements. In addition to research on seismic technology and means to investigate alleged uses of chemical weapons, this service is looking into the feasibility of a satellite
Income Tax
monitoring system to ensure compliance with arms control agreements. As I have already mentioned, it recently presented to the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva a working paper on the nature of the judicial system that might apply to space beyond the atmosphere.
The Department of External Affairs also gives a permanent $100,000 annual grant to the Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament. The Centre was established in 1983 and given the responsibility of organizing conferences and study groups on these questions.
The New Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security was created by Parliament in 1984 when all Parties supported the Bill shepherded by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Institute is directly funded by Parliament. Its budget in 1985-86 was $2.5 million and will increase to $5 million between now and 1988-89. It will seek to improve the knowledge and understanding of questions related to international peace and security within a Canadian context, and it will promote, finance and conduct research in those fields.
In 1983, 1984 and 1985 Canada gave a $100,000 grant to the World Disarmament Campaign. Our contributions will directly support world-wide public information and research activities. Our 1985 contribution was used to publish the Disarmament Yearbook, to finance the United Nations Institute for Disarmament, and to replenish the Voluntary Fund for the U.N. Decade for Women which we are celebrating this year.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that the Government is actively engaged in promoting peace and has earmarked sizeable funds to that end. In our opinion, the current Income Tax Act enables us to look after all matters concerning peace and security without the need to resort to the kind of measure proposed in the motion now before the House.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INCOME TAX PROVISION OF FUNDING FOR PEACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our caucus I should like to respond to the very heartfelt, informative, interesting and innovative proposal put forward by the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). I believe that he captured in his remarks and in the intent of his motion a sense of concern or anxiety among Canadians far more than did the statement of the Government spokesperson who, in a somewhat self-satisfying way, said that enough was being done. The Hon. Member for Regina East properly captured the real feelings of people who say that not enough is being done, that far more must be done.
During the past year I had the opportunity to participate in the work of the Special Joint Committee on International Relations. We had the rare experience of visiting across the country and listening to literally thousands of Canadians present their concerns before the committee. It was instructive that the first person from whom we heard was a young school teacher in Halifax. He gave a very eloquent and moving

March 10, 1986
Income Tax
address on star wars. Afterward I asked him what prompted him to make a presentation. He said that he was a school teacher and that his students had asked him about star wars. He was embarrassed at the time not to know anything about it and started meeting around the kitchen table with his friends. The more he examined the matter, the more he learned and the more he became concerned. Every Wednesday night they met around the kitchen table and began developing a series of ideas, analyses and information. Finally he appeared before the committee last July when it was on the East Coast. He talked about what they as a small community in Pictou county felt about star wars. That was not an isolated incident. It happened in many communities across the country. People would appear before the committee and say that more must be done.
The Hon. Member for Regina East properly expressed the imbalance in our commitments. People look around and see enormous sums being spent on armaments and in the nuclear arms race. They see the United States and the Soviet Union about to launch a new generation of the arms race with the proliferation and pollution of our outer space and the star wars program. They ask whether Canada can do more, whether we can find a way to turn the corner in a more meaningful way.
I am not saying that many of the efforts described by the Parliamentary Secretary are not useful. Of course they are useful, but they do not touch the deep undercurrent of unease and anxiety or that of hope and aspirations. Canadians believe that their country should be a peacemaker. As well, many people are asking what they can do to make a contribution, to do more.
I was partly dismayed at the committee hearing when we heard from the educators for nuclear responsibility, a group of school teachers from across the country. They said something which was very disturbing to me. They pointed out how difficult it was in the curricula of our high schools to get courses on arms control or on peace because they are considered by the school boards to be too controversial. Perhaps they represent too much of one side of the argument. When 1 visit the high schools in my riding every two or three weeks, 1 find that the students want to talk about one issue only. They do not want to talk about jobs. They do not want to talk about the environment, although they are concerned about it. They want to talk about the nuclear issue. Last Friday I visited Miles Macdonell Collegiate in my riding which was having a five-day teach-in on the issue of peace. They invited Members of Parliament to talk to them about what we thought was happening or where we could go. I was struck by the deep level of concern and by the willingness on the part of these young people to commit themselves. It is felt by thousands of Canadians that more must be done.
Does the legislative proposal of the Hon. Member for Regina East properly give form and substance to what must be done? In part I am attracted to the idea, but I have reservations on one ground-I think it would let the Government off the hook. If we resort to a form of populism or participatory democracy in the classical Greek sense where individuals make
up their own minds-and I do not object to that-it means that the Government of Canada loses its obligation to make a choice for Canadians. That is what Parliament is all about. I want the Government to make different choices. I want Members on both sides to make different choices. I believe we are not making the right choices any longer. We should have the opportunity to debate the Estimates of the Department of National Defence. The defence Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) should appear before the committee to explain their actions because they can easily forgo, evade or avoid their sense of responsibility.
I should like to refer to an example. Recently we received a report of the committee of NORAD which recommended that we sign up for another five years. To my unhappiness they indicated that there was not sufficient evidence to register a concern about the shifting sense of strategic thinking in the United States, moving from a sense of deterrence toward an active defence system. There was a multitude of testimony to show that this is what in fact was taking place. The Americans are making major commitments here and now to a very active defence system which will result in the fundamental militarization of Canadian territory, a vast network of active defence systems. That is a choice which Canadians should be making. It should not be made for us. It should not be made piecemeal. It should not be made in Washington. It should not be made in the NORAD headquarters. It should be made in this Parliament. However, it will only be made if Canadians understand what is going on. This means that the Government has to rid itself of its secretive attitude about what is taking place and start divulging far more of what it knows about the plans.
We must also look at the alternatives. If we say to the Americans, who are our allies, that we will not fully integrate our defence system with theirs if they go ahead with star wars, it means that we must put something in its place. We must put forward an alternative for the northern part of North America. As the Senate recommended a few years back, perhaps we must have our own form of satellite detection. We must develop an alternative to the proposals being put forward by the United States Defence Command. That is the important choice. It may mean that we have to utilize defence expenditures in a different way. We may not have to utilize them in a conventional or routine sense of going along with the conventional wisdom. We may have to establish a more independent defence posture in order that we can provide a bargaining position, a sense of leverage, with the United States in this very important and very crucial strategic security choice.
If the Hon. Member had his way and all those good minded Canadians who are very concerned about the arms race in effect abdicated and pulled out their money, there might not be money to provide the counterweight or counter ploy to the star wars program. That is a choice which should be retained in the hands of the Government, and it should be answerable for it. I agree fully with the stated purpose of the Hon. Member, that much more must go into the research and development of alternative techniques. One of the last acts of the Liberal Government, of which I was very proud, was the
March 10, 1986

establishment of the Canadian Peace Institute with an endowment of $5 million. I am pleased to say that the successor Government continued with that initiative. However, it is not enough; it is just a beginning.
Let us look at the tremendous appetite or hunger on the part of Canadians for more information. There is a tremendous ability in the number of peace groups across the country; there is individual time and talent; there are our educators and numbers of groups, ploughshare groups and others; and there is a kind of force they could bring to bear. We must find a better way of financing their efforts, a far more independent way so that they do not feel totally beholden to the Government. There must be an independent body which provides them with funding. They must feel far more free to undertake the kinds of investigation about which the Hon. Member talked. I fully agree with him. I would be prepared to say that perhaps we should look at the tax system to see if a more generous deduction could be allowed. It could be similar to the system of financing political Parties; that might be an alternative. I am not here to prescribe it, but 1 am saying that it is worthy of examination.
1 see the Chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence sitting opposite. Perhaps he would be prepared to take the question of peace education as part of his agenda for the committee in years ahead. It is critical and Canadians want it. However, if we follow the total advice of the Hon. Member, although I fully agree with his intent, in a sense we may be denying ourselves in Parliament the responsibility we need to make some very fundamental choices. For that reason, I express that reservation without expressing any reservation whatsoever about the intent, purpose, and objective of what he does.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, having expressed that reservation, we must still recognize that it is time for Parliament to have a much broader and more significant debate about the arms race and what we are doing, as a country, in the nuclear age. Canadians are far ahead of their Governments and this Parliament in expressing their concerns. They are leading us. One of the reasons is that we have not had an opportunity in this House to have a full-scaled broad-based debate about where Canada will go in the 1990s with regard to the matters of which the Parliamentary Secretary spoke, but which we have had very little opportunity to debate in the House.
I again recommend that Members of the Government side, who I know also feel very deeply about these concerns, represent to their caucus that it is time for Parliament to provide some leadership rather than to follow. It is time to let individual Members speak their minds and fully express what is in their hearts on this very fundamental issue. I compliment the Member for Regina East for at least giving us an hour of parliamentary time to do that. I wish we had an hour every day to do this. 1 wish this were an ongoing debate. If we had an ongoing debate, we may be able to accomplish what so many Canadians, particularly young Canadians, want us to do.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   INCOME TAX PROVISION OF FUNDING FOR PEACE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate. The issues raised by this motion are important and fundamental. For that reason, I do not apologize if my remarks today are similar to those expressed in this House last September 26 when we debated virtually the same proposal.
I have concerns about this proposition, albeit not about the ultimate goal of promoting peace and disarmament. It would be hard to take issue with the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) on that most desirable objective. However, the method he is proposing in this motion is not one which this House should adopt. There are important issues of tax policy and fiscal policy which argue against adoption of this particular proposition. There are also important questions of parliamentary democracy which are involved, questions about the way in which our society tries to live together and govern itself.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I will not hesitate to be repetitive today and to discuss the same issues as we debated last September on a similar motion of the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly). The sponsor of today's motion was repetitive in the same way. I can only regret that our arguments of six months ago did not succeed in changing his mind. We will try again today.
First, I would like to deal with an unfortunate implication in the wording of this motion. It contains the idea that somewhere there is a fundamental opposition between the search for peace and disarmament and our expenditures on defence. What kind of conclusion is a taxpayer likely to reach if, on his T-l tax return form, we present him with the option of earmarking 10 per cent of his income tax, or whatever percentage of federal spending goes to defence, to be spent instead on peace and disarmament, research and education? Is the taxpayer not likely to conclude that these two fields, defence and peace, are considered by the Government to be diametrically opposed?
I am in no way arguing that a valid case cannot be made for conscientious objectors, those who for strongly-held personal principles are opposed to serving in active combat where they could be called on to take another's life in defence of their country. However, that is in wartime. We are at peace now, and there is no contradiction in the position taken by the Government and accepted by a great majority in this House and across the country that our defence dollars are being spent to maintain peace and to prevent war.
Our defence expenditures reflect the long-standing Canadian policy in support of national and international security. For
years Canada has played an honourable international role in

seeking peaceful settlements of conflicts between countries. Our support of NATO and NORAD reflects the broadly-based public recognition that those alliances serve to enhance international security. I recognize that the New Democratic Party does not accept that position and would have Canada withdraw from the western alliance. However, 1 do not think that their position goes so far as to call for abolition of Canada's defence forces. This motion does not advocate such an extreme step. I think the reason for that is clear. The NDP, like the rest of us, recognize that our defence forces serve Canada's vital national interests in many ways.
If the New Democrats, by some strange chance, were ever called upon to form a government here, I wonder whether that Government would really adopt the principles which this motion advocates. This motion calls for a system of opting out which involves an issue that affects our national well-being in a very vital way. I do not think that this way of doing things is part of our system of parliamentary democracy. In our society, democracy involves much more than just the idea that the majority rules and imposes its view on the minority. Canadians have always sought tolerance. Through public debate we have sought to develop policies which take differing views into account, and we seek solutions with which everyone can live.
In the debate last September 26 on his motion, which is virtually the same as the one before us, the NDP Member cited the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. He argued that freedom of conscience and religion, as protected in the Charter, should allow citizens to opt out in this way from financial support of a major sector of Government activity. I remind the House that the rights and freedoms in the Charter are conditional. They are "subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society".
In our democratic society, we are all subject to reasonable limits on our freedom of conscience, religion, and self-expression. This simply means that tolerance must work both ways. The majority must be prepared to listen to individual differences, but at the same time the individual must recognize that there have to be broadly-accepted rules which apply to all in our society. I do not believe it is unreasonable to expect all citizens to bear their fair share of the cost of Government services provided for the common good. It is not unreasonable to say that a democratic Government should decide, in the final analysis, where and how those public funds are spent. I reemphasize that in our democratic society those decisions are made after the widest public debate with sensitivity to differing viewpoints.
The premise of this motion would allow any special interest group in the country to put forward a similar motion. If they were against abortion, they would want their funds to be earmarked for anti-abortion programs. If they were in favour of capital punishment, they would want their funds to be earmarked for that purpose. There are many special interest groups which would like to have their tax dollars earmarked for their special projects. Yet, we are faced with the reality of having to maintain the defence of the country. The previous
Government took the strict diplomatic route and totally ignored the physical defences by which we maintain the safety of the country.
We must remember that the Russians understand only one thing; a position of strength rather than weakness. If you have any doubt, talk to Poland, East Germany, the Ukraine, Hungary, or Czechoslovakia. These countries lost their freedom to the Soviet Union, which has very little sympathy at the negotiating table for the rights and liberties of the people in these countries. It is vital to the safety and well-being of our country that we ensure that we are wise stewards of our tax dollars. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the best position for peace is a position of strength. If we do not prepare adequate defences for the country, we could find ourselves in the same predicament as so many other countries find themselves.

subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL COMMISSION-LOCATION OF NEW UNITED STATES EMBASSY
NATIONAL CAPITAL COMMISSION-LOCATION OF NEW UNITED STATES EMBASSY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is my first experience with an adjournment debate as a follow-up to my question on February 24 to the Acting Minister of Public Works and I intend to get to the heart of my extremely serious concern quite quickly.
The National Capital Commission will be making a fundamental planning and political error if it recommends to the Government that the Mile Circle be used to house embassies. The local, regional, and indeed national outcry of total opposition to this proposal should in itself be a proper, clear, concise message to the Commission that it is making a big mistake. The duly-elected representatives of the four levels of Government directly affected are unanimously opposed to the proposal. Those representatives are myself at the federal level, Mr. Gilles Morin, the provincial Member, Mr. Marc Lavi-olette, the local alderman, and the Reeve of Rockcliffe Village which borders on the site, Mr. Pat Murray. There is no local political will for this project, why should there be a bureaucratic administrative one?
The Mile Circle land has been held in trust since 1904 by the federal Government as parkland. I cannot believe that today, in 1986, with all of our collective knowledge and experience, that the Commission is actually threatening to
March 10, 1986

destroy these parklands. 1 cannot accept the arguments that any development will be done in such a way as to maintain open spaces and a parkland setting. That is impossible since thousands and thousands of tons of concrete and steel will be sewn together by architects, engineers and construction workers to build embassies on the Mile Circle.
My professional background is in conservation and tourism development, and I know what impact infrastructures can have on parkland. If parks are for people, and I truly believe they are, then you put any or all development outside of them. Thomas Keefer meant for the Mile Circle to be used by people-people of all ages and from all places, not just from the National Capital region. The National Capital Act of 1958, Section 10(1) states:
The objects and purposes of the Commission are to prepare plans for and assist in the development, conservation and improvement of the National Capital region in order that the nature and character of the seat of the Government of Canada may be in accordance with its national significance.
I have received letters from across Canada opposed to this proposal from Canadians who feel that the Commission is compromising one of its fundamental philosophies, namely to conserve many of the natural parkland settings of our great capital. 1 am very proud of our magnificent city and 1 credit the Commission with making it that way. I, for one, want to keep it that way. In 1972 I defended Banff National Park from being raped by tourist developers. As someone who has lived in Ottawa all my life, I am proud to defend the Mile Circle Park from being raped by the Commission. This act of short-sightedness must be stopped. There are certain sections of our city that are sacrosanct, and this is one of them.
The Policy for Parkways and Driveways, published by the NCC as approved in July, 1984, the official plan of the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton as approved by the Province of Ontario in November, 1983, and the official plan of land use of the City of Ottawa, published in June, 1984, all state their commitment to the public open-space corridor along the Ottawa River, with the Mile Circle as part of this landscape conservation. These are commitments made to their constituents by three levels of Government. If the federal Government places embassy offices on this land, it would be an expression of contempt for the due process of planning.
Treasury Board wants to raise new revenue by selling some land, and I think we will all agree that this is worth while. However, for the sake of financial expediency, this particular case is not in the national interest. Is the NCC willing to reopen the terms of reference for the contract to study the Mile Circle site so that it would include the study of other potential sites as well? Will the Commission be willing to consult or will it not consult beforehand with community groups on such projects?
Is the Commission prepared to put its final selections through the due rezoning process required of all other citizens by the City of Ottawa and the Province of Ontario? If not, what form is there for the citizens of this region to participate in major rezoning projects by the Commission? Will the
Adjournment Debate
Commission seriously consider an appropriate site on the Rockcliffe Air Base as a timely alternative to the Mile Circle? My last question is: Will the consultant report on this proposal be made public?
In conclusion, let me congratulate the tremendous efforts of the Save the Mile Circle Committee for their work, and to my executive in Ottawa-Carleton for unanimously supporting my opposition to this project. If this proposal is part of the vision for our capital, then I cannot see very clearly.

subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL COMMISSION-LOCATION OF NEW UNITED STATES EMBASSY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to first compliment my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner), for his diligence and commitment not only to this House, but outside the House and in caucus. His record is well known to his constituents.
As you know, there are no simple solutions to a complex issue such as the site for the U.S. embassy. The process that we are going through is lengthy. We are dealing with an issue of major national importance. We are also dealing with the very real concerns that were expressed and which all committees face in an evolving capital city. All of us need to share the responsibilities as well as the benefits of living in a capital city in the late 20th century. The relocation of the American embassy has a very long history. I do not want to bore Members with the endlessly long details of the events which followed the evolution of this issue, but I would like to point out a couple of significant highlights and events.
The relocation of the embassy first arose in 1969 when the embassy proposed to expand its facilities along Wellington Street to meet the growing accommodation requirements. However, this property was considered to be of paramount importance in meeting the accommodation needs of Parliament. The Government of Canada subsequently proposed to find another site to which the American embassy could be relocated. As the federal Government's agent responsible for creation of the capital, the National Capital Commission was charged with finding an appropriate site.
Until about a year ago, it was considered that a top priority site would be the one on Sussex Drive, north of the Connaught building. However, the U.S. Government imposed regulations for locating new embassy buildings. Obviously we know why. The NCC was asked to add additional criteria to the list for site selection. These new criteria for site selection included among others: a minimum site area requirement of at least six to eight acres; no tall buildings adjacent; and a buffer zone all around the embassy.
In all, 12 major criteria were used in evaluating some 20 sites in both the Quebec and Ontario parts of the National Capital Region. During the process of site evaluation, a certain number of sites were rapidly eliminated. Selections of these sites would throw into question a number of long established fundamental capital planning principles, as pointed out by my colleague. These principles include, among others, preservation of our river front properties. This exclusion is consistent with the NCC long-standing policy to retain federal river front land

March 10, 1986
Adjournment Debate
in Canadian ownership for public use. This policy acts to ensure direct access by the public to the river shore. The remaining candidate sites were considered in detail, and the Mile Circle was selected as the site which best met all criteria.
As part of the site selection process, the NCC has retained the services of a consultant charged with carrying on a detailed site analysis. This analysis includes such matters as the suitability of land use arrangements in the Mile Circle, environmental impact, landscape design and ecological considerations. The study should be completed by spring. At that time the NCC intends to recommend a specific site in the Mile Circle area. The Canadian Government may then exchange this site with the American Government for the U.S. embassy land and buildings on Wellington Street.
It is my sincere hope that at the end of this process we will have produced a site development concept for the Mile Circle which enables the Government to meet its national and international obligations. I am sure that I need not remind my hon. colleagues that the Government of the United States spared no effort in providing our own Government with one of the most prestigious sites for our embassy in the City of Washington. In this context, I would call on the citizens of this great capital city to recognize their shared role and responsibility in this international dimension of the capital.

Mr. Speaker, a while ago 1 asked the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) about the Government's plans to continue providing strong encouragement for the cultural heritages of immigrants to Canada. The Minister assured me of the Government's commitment to retention of cultural heritages, and that he was in the process of reviewing the funding criteria for those programs encouraging the retention of ethnic culture.
Multiculturalism is a very important aspect of our lives. In fact, multiculturalism is part of what it means to be Canadian. In my riding of Don Valley East, one of its most exciting features is the cultural diversity.
My wife, Sandy, and I can recount many close friends from varying cultural backgrounds. George and Penny Poulos are of Greek heritage. Jay and Ann Hong are from South Korea. Rhett and Betsy Abarquez's roots are in the Philippines. Incidentally, one can imagine how thrilled they are with the new democratic Government of President Corazon Aquino. Garo and Zaro Pashayan are proud of their Armenian heritage. Mrs. Setsuko Thurlow of Olsen Drive is a survivor of Hiroshima. Frank and Judy Wilson are recognized leaders in the Jewish community. Vincent and Agnes Ching cherish their Chinese heritage, having been born in Hong Kong. George and Margaret Hayling from the black community take great pride in being from Barbados.
The peaceful coexistence of people of diverse races and
cultures, bonded by common citizenship, not only fosters social
cohesion and national unity, but also creates the basis for the
eradication of prejudice and bigotry. The cultural diversity of Canada is as much a part of our national identity as regional diversity.
This diversity has been a factor throughout the history of Canada. Our nation was founded on the basis of cultural pluralism. The subsequent arrival of immigrants from many countries added to the pluralistic nature of the developing Canadian society.
The multicultural nature of Canadian society was officially recognized in 1971, when the House of Commons gave unanimous consent to the Government's response of the 1969 report on the "Cultural Contribution of the Other Ethnic Groups" of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism established in 1962.
The Government adopted an official policy of multiculturalism within a bilingual framework. In 1972, the Multicultural Directorate was established within the Department of the Secretary of State, and a Minister of State for Multiculturalism was appointed. In 1973, the Canadian Consultative Council on Multiculturalism was established. In 1983, this Council was revitalized and restructured to become the Canadian Multiculturalism Council, or the CMC.
In 1982 the Charter of Rights and Freedoms was proclaimed. Section 27 reads: "This Charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians".
In May of 1985, the first deferal/provincial/territorial conference on multiculturalism was held. Employment Equity legislation was passed by the House of Commons. Also, in response to the recommendations of the "Equality for All" report of the Special Parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights, a Standing Committee on Multiculturalism was established. With the inception of this committee, everything pertaining to multiculturalism can be examined in depth. The mandate, to encourage and monitor the implementation of the principles of the multiculturalism policy throughout the Government of Canada, is a great responsibility and, indeed, a great opportunity. I am proud to be a founding member of this Standing Committee.
The Government's policy on multiculturalism is to help to preserve and enhance the traditional cultures; help members of the enthocultural minorities to develop the skills they need to participate fully in Canadian society and the economy; help all Canadians to recognize the multicultural nature of the country and to adapt themselves and their institutions accordingly. This provides a solid framework for all Canadians.

Canadians are proud of their origins and cultural heritage and wish to retain this essential part of their identity. The retention of cultural heritage is very important, not only to the various ethnocultural groups but to Canadian society as a whole. We are all enriched by cultural diversity. Indeed, our own family is expanding its cultural roots. While Sandy's parents were born in Scotland, my mother is of Irish descent and my father of English descent. Our younger daughter,
March 10, 1986

Leslie, married John Strolenberg, who was born in Holland. Our elder daughter, Pamela, married Mark Zaorski, who is of Polish-lrish heritage. Therefore we are developing a rich diversity within our own growing family.
As the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek) has pointed out recently, multiculturalism encompasses all aspects of our lives. It has to do with jobs and rights as well as cultural retention. It must become both a social and economic reality. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has stated, and I quote:
There is no obligation more compelling, no duty more irresistable than to ensure that our minorities live at all times in conditions of fairness and justice.
It is a cornerstone of multicultural policy that there shall be no barriers to prevent Canadians, whatever their origins, from enjoying all the rights and privileges of citizenship.
In closing, may I say that the Minister of State for Multiculturalism in recent statements has spoken about the need to bring ethnic minorities more fully into the economic mainstream of Canada. Multiculturalism, in addition to its widely perceived value as a cultural asset, also makes good business sense. It is also a decisive advantage in a highly competitive economic environment. One way to create economic opportunity is to take greater advantage of the talents and resources of our ethnocultural communities. Over half of all small businesses in Canada are run by members of ethnocultural communities. In recognition of this fact, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism is sponsoring a conference in April called "Multuralism Means Business". I am very proud to be a part of this Government for its initiative in the field of multiculturalism and I look forward to even greater things to come.
